## The Hubble Space Telescope: A Revolutionary Observatory

The Hubble Space Telescope (HST) is one of NASA's most significant scientific instruments, launched into low Earth orbit on April 24, 1990, aboard Space Shuttle Discovery. Named after astronomer Edwin Hubble, the telescope features a 2.4-meter mirror and five main instruments that observe in the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. Its position outside Earth's atmosphere allows it to capture extraordinarily high-resolution images with minimal background light, producing some of the most detailed visible light images ever recorded and enabling a deep view into space.

The telescope's journey to success was not without challenges. Originally intended for launch in 1983, the project faced technical delays, budget problems, and was further postponed following the 1986 Challenger disaster. After its 1990 launch, scientists discovered that the main mirror had been ground incorrectly, causing spherical aberration that severely compromised the telescope's capabilities. This flaw was corrected during a servicing mission (STS-61) in 1993, and Hubble has since become the only telescope designed to be maintained in space by astronauts. Five Space Shuttle missions have repaired, upgraded, and replaced systems on the telescope, with the final servicing mission completed in 2009.

Hubble's discoveries have fundamentally transformed our understanding of the universe. One of its primary achievements was measuring the Hubble constant—the rate at which the universe is expanding—with unprecedented accuracy of ±10%, compared to previous estimates with errors up to 50%. This refined measurement established that the universe is approximately 13.7 billion years old. ## The Great Barrier Reef: A Natural Wonder Under Threat

The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest reef system, stretching 2,300 kilometres along the east coast of Australia from Cape York to Bundaberg. Composed of roughly 2,900 individual reefs and 940 islands and cays, it covers approximately 344,400 square kilometres in the Coral Sea off Queensland. This extraordinary ecosystem supports remarkable biodiversity, including more than 1,500 fish species, 30 species of cetaceans, six species of sea turtles, 215 bird species, and close to 5,000 mollusc species. The reef's islands and waters provide critical breeding grounds for millions of birds and marine animals, making it one of Earth's most biologically significant ecosystems.

However, the Great Barrier Reef faces mounting environmental pressures. According to the Australian Government's Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority (GBRMPA), climate change is the most significant threat. Rising sea temperatures pose a particular danger—reef scientist Terry Done has predicted that a one-degree rise in global temperature would result in 82% of the reef being bleached, while a three-degree rise would cause total coral mortality. A 2009 GBRMPA report warned that if carbon dioxide levels reached 450 parts per million, corals and reef habitats would become highly vulnerable.

Water quality degradation represents another major threat. The reef's catchment area covers 423,000 square kilometres and includes major urban centers like Cairns and Townsville, as well as extensive agricultural operations. Over 90% of nutrient pollution during tropical flood events comes from farms, and approximately 700 of the 3,000 reefs are in risk zones where water quality has declined due to chemical runoff and sediment.
